title: Statistics & Probability: Data, Distributions & Inference
description: Explore essential mathematical concepts through carefully crafted questions. Strengthen your understanding, practice your reasoning, and learn at your own pace.

questions.learningObjective: Use combinations to count equally likely outcomes for probability calculations.
questions.question: A learner reports 21 for this situation. Which option gives the correct result instead? A committee of 3 people is chosen at random from a group of 7 candidates. How many different committees are possible?
questions.explanation: Key idea: a committee is an unordered selection, so changing the order does not create a new outcome. Applying that principle to the data given in the question leads to option A, 35. Common trap: using permutations when the selected people have no positions or roles. Check: the count should be an integer and cannot exceed the number of ordered selections.
questions.hint: Step 1: identify the quantity or decision being asked for. Step 2: choose the definition or formula that matches the setting. Common trap: using permutations when the selected people have no positions or roles.

questions.learningObjective: Test whether two events are independent by comparing P(A)P(B) to P(A and B).
questions.question: For this statistical task, identify the appropriate calculation and determine the requested result. Two events have \(P(A)\) = 0.34, \(P(B)\) = 0.33, and \(P(A\cap B)\) = 0.1122. Are A and B independent?

options.label: A
options.text: No, because \(P(A)P(B)\) does not equal \(P(A\cap B)\)

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, because \(P(A)\) + \(P(B)\) = \(P(A\cap B)\)

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because \(P(A)P(B)\) = \(P(A\cap B)\)

questions.explanation: Key idea: independence means knowing one event occurs does not change the probability of the other. Applying that principle to the data given in the question leads to option C, Yes, because \(P(A)P(B)\) = \(P(A\cap B)\). Common trap: confusing independence with mutual exclusivity. Check: test \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\); addition is not the independence criterion.
questions.hint: Step 1: identify the quantity or decision being asked for. Step 2: choose the definition or formula that matches the setting. Common trap: confusing independence with mutual exclusivity.

questions.concept: Confidence interval for a mean (sigma unknown)
questions.learningObjective: Construct a t-based confidence interval for a population mean when sigma is unknown.
questions.question: A random sample of size \(n=20\) has sample mean \(\bar{x}=53\) and sample standard deviation \(s=8\). Since \(\sigma\) is unknown, construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean using the t-distribution (\(t_{\alpha/2,19}=2.093\)).
questions.explanation: Check: the interval is centered at \(\bar{x}\) and has equal-width endpoints. Applying that principle to the data given in the question leads to option B, (49.26, 56.74). Key idea: when \(\sigma\) is unknown, the sample standard deviation \(s\) is used with a \(t\)-critical value and \(n-1\) degrees of freedom. Common trap: substituting a \(z\)-critical value when the problem explicitly calls for the \(t\)-distribution.
questions.hint: Step 1: identify the quantity or decision being asked for. Step 2: choose the definition or formula that matches the setting. Key idea: when \(\sigma\) is unknown, the sample standard deviation \(s\) is used with a \(t\)-critical value and \(n-1\) degrees of freedom.

Common trap: forgetting the combinatorial factor that counts where the successes can occur.

questions.concept: Decision rule for a two-tailed test
questions.learningObjective: Apply the critical-value decision rule to reach a conclusion in a hypothesis test.
questions.question: In a two-tailed z-test at significance level \(\alpha\) = 0.05, the computed test statistic is \(z=2.84\). The critical values are \(\pm\)1.96. What is the correct decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Reject \(H_0\)

options.label: B
options.text: Fail to reject \(H_0\)

options.label: C
options.text: Accept \(H_a\) as proven true

questions.explanation: Common trap: comparing \(z\) without taking its absolute value, or using a one-tailed cutoff. Applying that principle to the data given in the question leads to option A, Reject \(H_0\). Check: reject when \(\lvert z\rvert\) exceeds the positive critical value. Key idea: in a two-tailed test, evidence in either direction can lead to rejection.
questions.hint: Step 1: identify the quantity or decision being asked for. Step 2: choose the definition or formula that matches the setting. Check: reject when \(\lvert z\rvert\) exceeds the positive critical value.

Applying that principle to the data given in the question leads to option A, 3.571. Key idea: for Poisson data, the MLE of \(\lambda\) is the sample mean. Common trap: dividing the total count by the wrong sample size or treating \(\lambda\) as a variance estimate only.

questions.learningObjective: Use a p-value to make a decision relative to a stated significance level.

options.text: Reject \(H_0\), since the p-value is less than \(\alpha\)

Check: compare the p-value with \(\alpha\); do not reverse the inequality. Key idea: a p-value measures how incompatible the observed test statistic is with \(H_0\), under the test model.
